events.title: The Council of Pisa elects a third claimant
events.shortBlurb: Seeking to end the Western Schism, the council deposed two rival popes and elected a third, deepening the crisis…
body: Since 1378 the Western Schism had divided Latin Christendom between rival popes at Rome and Avignon. When neither Gregory XII nor Benedict XIII would give way, cardinals of both obediences abandoned them and, meeting at Livorno in 1408, summoned a general council to Pisa.

The council opened in the cathedral on 25 March 1409 with some five hundred fathers — cardinals, bishops, doctors, and ambassadors of the Christian princes. On 5 June it deposed both claimants, and on 26 June elected in their stead Peter Philargos, a Franciscan of Crete and cardinal of Milan, who took the name Alexander V.

The two deposed popes each kept an obedience of kingdoms, so that Christendom now counted three rival lines. Alexander V died at Bologna within the year, and his successor, Baldassare Cossa, ruled as John XXIII; the Pisan line is reckoned among the antipopes. The schism was healed only at Constance, by the election of Martin V in 1417.
